200 years from a block of wood on a cartwheel to cars that brake by themselves.

1869 · Air stops a train (George Westinghouse)
1902 · The disc brake is patented (Frederick W. Lanchester)
1917 · Fluid in place of rods (Malcolm Loughead (later spelled Lockheed))
1953 · Disc brakes win Le Mans (Tony Rolt and Duncan Hamilton, Jaguar and Dunlop)
1968 · Two circuits, by law (U.S. Department of Transportation)
1978 · Electronic ABS goes on sale (Bosch and Mercedes-Benz)

captions.instagram:
How do brakes work?

Your foot pushes with 100 newtons and the pads squeeze with 7,000. Follow the push through a lever, a vacuum servo and Pascal's law, watch a disc soak up the heat of a stop, and see ABS catch a locking wheel on a wet road.

→ A 1,200 kg car at 100 km/h carries 463 kJ. Brakes turn every joule of it into heat.
→ Two separate circuits, split diagonally: burst one pipe and half the braking is still there.
→ The pedal is a 4 to 1 lever, and a vacuum servo triples the push again.
→ Pascal's law: the same pressure on a piston six times bigger gives six times the force.
→ A floating caliper has one piston, yet squeezes the disc from both sides with equal force.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/brakeclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How do brakes work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Your foot pushes with 100 newtons and the pads squeeze with 7,000. Follow the push through a lever, a vacuum servo and Pascal's law, watch a disc soak up the heat of a stop, and see ABS catch a locking wheel on a wet road.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/brakeclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/brakeclear

In this video:
• Brakes turn motion into heat. A 1,200 kg car at 100 km/h carries 463 kJ of kinetic energy.
• A 100 N push becomes 7 kN. The pedal is a 4 to 1 lever.
• Discs pinch, drums push out. A floating caliper has one piston but squeezes the disc from both sides, and its square rubber seal pulls the pads clear again.
• Heat is the limit. One hard stop from 100 km/h warms each 5 kg front rotor by about 65 °C.
• A tyre grips best while it still turns. Grip peaks at about 10 to 20% slip.
• Air that fails safe, motors that give back. Trucks and buses brake with compressed air, and a strong spring in each chamber applies the brakes if the air is lost.
